Afshin

messages.body_plain:
Dear researchers and mirt enthusiasts,

We would like to extend an invitation to researchers interested in utilizing our database of a free IQ test, available on https://www.brght.org. With over 3,000 questions in 16 subcategories, our test has been taken by over 600,000 people in the last six months alone.

Our mission is to provide the most accurate online IQ test in the world, and we believe that making our anonymized data available to researchers is the most efficient way to achieve this goal. As such, we thought this Google Group would be the perfect place to share this invitation with researchers who may be interested in working with our data.

Our test is adaptive and allows everyone 20 minutes to answer 30 questions, with difficulty levels increasing until the user has a ~50% chance of answering correctly. You can try the test for yourself at brght.org/start <http://brght.org/start> or visit the links below to view examples of the questions we ask.

https://brght.org/question/S2SbTj5j/
https://brght.org/question/3GNjnQVq/
https://brght.org/question/bh7xmjB4/
https://brght.org/question/cZ2ZyCZo/
https://brght.org/question/7rQ9ANyH/
https://brght.org/question/cBm2Lxia/

To view what data is available, please visit our website's dedicated page for researchers at https://brght.org/data-request/. If you are interested, feel free to reply to this post or write me a pm.

We have used the MIRT package ourselves to perform a Rash, 2PL, and 3PL model on the last 50,000 results. While we acknowledge our limited knowledge of IRT models, the results of our analysis seem promising. However, we struggle to quantify the quality of the models due to the M2 function's inability to handle missing response patterns, while each response pattern only contains 30 non-empty (NA) values out of 3000+ items.

Thank you for your time and consideration. We look forward to hearing from you and potentially working together in the future!

Kind regards,

Jacques Huppes

Using mixedmirt function, I can include both item covariates (aka explanatory LLTM model) and person covariates (aka latent regression). However, I need to include some interaction between person and item.

I can estimate the model using lme4 package, but mirt provides me the possibility to estimate 2PL model and get fit indices (M2 statistics). Is there any way to do it in mirt?
Hynek

And I'm not sure ltm would be the best for DIF analyses (would require ad-hoc equating rather than direct model fitting). It's a free world though, so go with whatever you feel is appropriate.

Phil

Hi Yale,

I believe this is expected behaviour with no work around. The WLE estimator requires computing the determinant of the observed information matrix which, for the testlet model and friends, is non-positive definite given the implied constraints. You should have seen many warnings pop up in your R console to indicate this information. Hence, for these particularly constrained models you'll have to stick with some of the more basic estimators for now (I'd recommend MAPs). HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
I assume your other model is a confirmatory item factor analysis model, so I'll respond under that assumption.

In general, I wouldn't treat exploratory factor models in the same way as confirmatory ones. The former are highly over-parameterized and subject to rotational indeterminacy, so the correlation will be a function of what rotation you pick and under what criteria. EFAs are largely meant to be suggestive of underlying factor patterns and relationships but not definitive. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Aiden,

Of course. Here's how you can do this using the LR or Wald tests.

library(mirt)
set.seed(12345)
a <- matrix(abs(rnorm(15,1,.3)), ncol=1)
d <- matrix(rnorm(15,0,.7),ncol=1)
itemtype <- rep('2PL', nrow(a))
N <- 1000
dataset1 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype)
dataset2 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype, mu = .1, sigma = matrix(1.5))
dat <- rbind(dataset1, dataset2)
group <- c(rep('D1', N), rep('D2', N))

#equal intercepts, free variance and means

mod_scalar2 <- multipleGroup(dat, group = group, SE=TRUE,

                             invariance=c('slopes', 'intercepts', 'free_var','free_means'))

mod_scalar1 <- multipleGroup(dat, group = group,
                             invariance=c('slopes', 'intercepts', 'free_var'))

coef(mod_scalar2, simplify=TRUE)
coef(mod_scalar1, simplify=TRUE)

# compared all at once (in order of most constrained to least)

anova(mod_scalar1, mod_scalar2)

# via wald test
wald(mod_scalar2)
wald(mod_scalar2, 'MEAN_1.123 = 0')

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Anchoring items manually vs. using multipleGroup vs. linking scores via plink
messages.subject_clean: Anchoring items manually vs. using multipleGroup vs. linking scores via plink
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ramin,

The multiple group IRT approach treats each group as a sample from a unique population, thereby allowing different properties to be compared across groups if sufficient anchoring is available. So, you'll notice that the latent mean/variance are different in the MG application compared to the standard 0-1 scaling in single group IRT models, which influences Bayes estimates in the fscores() function. If it helps, the single group IRT model is formally equivalent to a MG model when all the item parameters are constrained to be equal across groups (no DIF), and the latent distribution densities are constrained to be equal (e.g., 0-1). Hence, you can think of MG-IRT models as being a blend between the two modeling extremes "ignoring the group membership entirely" and fitting a single group IRT model without group information, and "taking data subsets and fitting single group IRTmodels", which is your 3). HTH.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: How to interpret LD standardised residuals
messages.body_plain:
Cutoffs are cutoffs; I don't enjoy them but I understand that some researchers like to rely on arbitrary lines in the sand for simplification. You could make similar claims for the Cramer's V outputs from mirt, though a simulation study would have to be run to determine reasonable cutoff locations for reporting. If it helps though, you can use the residuals(..., approx.z) argument to obtain the same standardized residuals in which the |10| cutoff would apply.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: traditional parameterization/plotting for multi-dimensional models
messages.body_plain:
They can, but not practically. The difficulty parameters reflect points of inflection in the probability functions, which for multidimensional models would be infinitely divisible vectors of difficulties relating to P(theta, a1, a2, d1) = .5. This is generally why the slope intercept version is preferred as they scale the probability functions in more reasonably anchored locations. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Handling items with different numbers of response categories
messages.subject_clean: Handling items with different numbers of response categories
messages.body_plain:
It's a tricky problem indeed. Low endorsement options are ripe with high sampling variability, so their use in models can be detrimental and lead to non-convergence issues. Bayes priors can help with this issue by including the researchers 'quasi prior data experience, if they are justifiable. Though I will note that missing observations on the extreme ends of responses (e.g., 1 or 5 in a five-point Likert scale) are less problematic than middle response options as in models like the GRM, where response functions are ordinal anyway, missing observations just mean the item was too difficult/easy and so any response bias due to these extreme categories is irrelevant anyway as it doesn't seem to be influencing any of the observations.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Handling items with different numbers of response categories
messages.body_plain:
There is a way to trick mirt into ghosting in response categories with the argument customK in the technical list. Though you'll have to be very careful in how you proceed as this gets into pretty tricky territory. The alternative way to do this that would better guarantee consistency would be to include the missing observations for one or more dummy response vectors and supply a survey.weight input to give these observations a weight of 0 and weigh all other observations accordingly to match the original sample demographics. Applying suitable constraints are still required though, so be warned that any ghosting approach will be filled with dragons....

Phil
